examples.knowledge_point: Determining where a Tangent Line Intersects an Axis
examples.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+4x$ at the point $(1,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4\sqrt{x}+4x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt{x}+4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{1/2}+4x) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m=f'(1) = 2(1)^{-1/2}+4 = 6.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =6(x-1) \\ y & =6x-6+8 \\ y & =6x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6x+2 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $\left(-\dfrac 1 3, 0\right).$

feedback.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x$ at the point $(1,9).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-5}+7x) \\  & =-10{x}^{-6}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-10(1{)}^{-6}+7=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=-3$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,9),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(9) & =-3(x-1) \\ y & =-3x+3+9 \\ y & =-3x+12.\end{aligned}
$$
